AI in AML: where banks use it and what to document

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•9 min read

AI in AML (artificial intelligence in anti-money laundering) is the use of machine learning and related techniques inside a bank's AML program: scoring and tuning transaction monitoring, matching names in sanctions screening, rating customer risk, sorting adverse media and helping investigators assemble cases. Since a 2018 joint statement, US banking agencies and FinCEN have welcomed innovation, including AI, in BSA/AML programs, and banks must still meet their BSA/AML obligations. For each use, the team should be able to explain it, show how it was validated and name who decides.

This guide covers each use, what to document and test, and who decides. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What AI in AML means

Much of the AI described in AML guidance is machine learning: statistical models trained on past data to score, rank or group. The FATF's 2021 report on new technologies describes unsupervised algorithms that group customers so controls such as "transaction threshold settings" fit each group, and alert scoring that helps teams focus. Natural language processing (NLP) reads text such as news, and fuzzy matching compares names spelled differently.

The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual draws a similar line. Rule-based systems flag transactions outside set rules, while "Intelligent systems are adaptive" and compare activity with history or a peer group. The interagency model risk guidance issued as SR 26-2 excludes "deterministic rule-based processes" from its definition of a model, and says its principles apply to "non-generative, non-agentic AI models." A fixed threshold rule may sit outside model risk management. A machine learning score that ranks alerts sits inside its definition of a model.

What regulators have said about artificial intelligence in AML

YearDocumentWhat it says about AI
2018Joint statement on innovative efforts (Fed, FDIC, FinCEN, NCUA, OCC)Some banks are "experimenting with artificial intelligence"; pilots alongside existing processes should not by themselves draw criticism.
2021Interagency request for information on AI (Fed, CFPB, FDIC, NCUA, OCC)Lists "Flagging unusual transactions" as a use; names explainability, data usage and dynamic updating as challenges.
2021FATF report on new technologies for AML/CFTA lack of explainability "can undermine" the ability to assess a tool, so that its effectiveness "cannot be established".
2024EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, Article 76(5)Allows automated and AI decisions on conditions, including human intervention and an explanation.
2026SR 26-2 (Fed, OCC, FDIC)Supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8; covers non-generative, non-agentic AI models, not generative or agentic AI.

The 2018 statement adds that when an AI-based monitoring pilot finds activity the existing process missed, "the Agencies will not automatically assume that the banks' existing processes are deficient."

Where AI is used in AML compliance

Each use, and what the bank should be able to show an examiner:

Program areaHow AI is usedWhat to document and testWho decides
Transaction monitoringScores and ranks alerts; groups customers to set thresholdsFiltering criteria, thresholds and why they fit the bank's risks; independent validationAn analyst closes or escalates each alert
Sanctions screeningFuzzy and NLP name matching to catch spelling variantsMatching criteria and sensitivity, set by risk; false hit volumesA reviewer decides whether a hit is a valid match
Customer risk ratingScores customers from due diligence dataThe factors used, how scores map to ratings, results checked against reviewed filesStaff approve rating changes and changes to due diligence
Adverse mediaNLP sorts news by relevance and links articles to customersSources searched, relevance rules, what was set aside and whyAn analyst judges whether an article is about the customer and matters
InvestigationsAssembles transactions, counterparties and documentsWhat was gathered and from which systemThe investigator draws the conclusion
Narrative draftingGenerative AI drafts case notes or narrative textThe draft, the edits and the facts it citesThe decision maker decides whether to file

AI in AML transaction monitoring

For monitoring, the FFIEC manual says management "should document and be able to explain filtering criteria, thresholds used, and how both are appropriate for the bank's risks." The system's "programming methodology and effectiveness should be independently validated". For a machine learning score, that points to:

  • what the score predicts, the data it uses and the threshold that sends an alert to review;
  • test results on alerts already worked, including those that ended in a SAR;
  • a change log for each retraining and threshold move, with the approver;
  • periodic re-testing, since management should "periodically review and test the filtering criteria and thresholds".

FATF says monitoring technology should, for the most part, stay inside a wider system with "an element of human analysis for specific alerts or areas of higher risk." The alert triage use case shows that handoff.

Screening and name matching

The FFIEC manual's OFAC section asks each bank to "clearly define its criteria for comparing names" on the OFAC list with names in its files. The sensitivity of screening software "should be based on a bank's assessment of its risk and the volume of its transactions", and "A high volume of false hits may indicate a need to review the bank's interdiction program." FATF notes that NLP and fuzzy matching can reduce false positives and false negatives in screening. The bank's procedures should also "address how it will determine whether an initial OFAC hit is a valid match or a false hit"; see our guide to sanctions screening.

Customer risk scoring and adverse media

The FFIEC manual's due diligence section expects the program to be "sufficiently detailed to distinguish between significant variations" in customer risk. There are "no required risk profile categories", so the bank sets and writes down how a score maps to a rating. Examiners "may review individual customer risk decisions", so keep the inputs behind each rating.

In the EU, under Article 76(5) of the AMLR, an automated or AI decision to enter, refuse or maintain a business relationship, or to increase or decrease due diligence, must be "subject to meaningful human intervention". The customer may obtain an explanation of the decision and challenge it, except in relation to a suspicion report under Article 69, so in practice the bank needs to be able to explain the decision, including what the model contributed. The regulation applies from July 10, 2027.

For adverse media, the 2021 RFI lists analysis of "news flow" among NLP uses, and FATF describes NLP tools "connecting search engine results with PEP lists". A model can sort and summarize; an analyst decides whether an article is about this customer and changes the risk. See the PEP and adverse media use case.

Investigation and narrative support

Generative AI tools can summarize a case file and draft notes or narrative text. The FFIEC manual says investigators "should document conclusions including any recommendation regarding whether or not to file a SAR", and gives the final filing decision to a decision maker with the authority to make it. Under 31 CFR 1020.320(e), a SAR "and any information that would reveal the existence of a SAR, are confidential", so treat any tool or vendor that sees SAR material as subject to that confidentiality. And with generative AI outside SR 26-2, the bank's own governance decides who checks each draft against the record and which data the tool may receive.

Where agentic AI fits

An AI agent runs a multi-step task, such as triaging an alert, across several systems and hands the result to an analyst. SR 26-2 places agentic AI outside its scope, so the procedure the agent follows, its stop points and its run log carry the governance. Our guide to agentic AI in AML covers that run step by step.

Model risk, explainability and data quality

The 2021 RFI named three areas where AI makes risk management harder: explainability, "Broader or More Intensive Data Usage" and dynamic updating, meaning approaches that can update themselves "sometimes without human interaction". Each has a counterpart in validation:

  • Explainability. The SR 26-2 guidance says conceptual soundness can be assessed through "interpretability measures or benchmarking to other models". The NIST AI Risk Management Framework asks that the model be "explained, validated, and documented".
  • Data. The RFI notes that an AI system "generally reflects any limitations of that dataset." FATF adds that errors in training data, including past false positives, get "trained-in" to the model.
  • Change. Under SR 26-2, ongoing monitoring checks performance given changes in "products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions."
  • Vendors. For vendor models, "the principles of model risk management remain applicable", and sound practice includes understanding the model's "conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance."

Our note on what SR 26-2 changes covers its scope and the end of SR 21-8, the 2021 statement on BSA/AML systems.

How a compliance team brings AI into the AML program

  1. Inventory it. NIST calls for mechanisms "to inventory AI systems". Record the owner, purpose and decisions touched, and classify each component as a model or a rule under SR 26-2.
  2. Write the decision boundary. State what the component may do (rank, group, draft) and what a named person must decide (close, escalate, file, change a rating).
  3. Check the data covers your customers and products, and record known gaps.
  4. Validate before use. Test against cases your team has already decided, including SARs filed, and run it in parallel with the existing process where you can.
  5. Monitor in production. Track how often reviewers agree with or overrule the output, and re-test after retraining, threshold changes or new data sources.
  6. Review vendors. The 2018 statement names third-party risk management, information security and privacy among the factors to address.

For procedure-driven work, Verkflo compiles a written procedure into a versioned spec, tests it with evals and sandbox runs before live use, and logs each run, with its review pauses, in a hash-chained audit log; see AML automation.

Will AI replace AML jobs?

The guidance assigns the decisions to people. The FFIEC manual expects a decision maker with authority over SAR filing, and asks banks to assign "adequate staff" who have "the requisite experience levels". The EU AMLR requires meaningful human intervention when automated or AI processes drive decisions on relationships and due diligence. NIST asks organizations to define "roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations". None of these documents forecasts staffing levels; each assigns the decision to a person.

Common questions

How is artificial intelligence used in anti-money laundering?

To rank alerts, set thresholds by customer group, match names, rate customer risk, sort adverse media and draft case notes, each with documentation, validation and a person over the decision.

Do regulators require banks to use AI for AML?

No. The 2018 joint statement says the agencies will not penalize or criticize banks with effective programs that choose not to pursue innovative approaches.

Is machine learning in AML covered by model risk guidance?

Under SR 26-2, non-generative, non-agentic AI models are in scope, deterministic rule-based processes are excluded, and generative and agentic AI are out of scope. The guidance is "expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets", though it may also be relevant to smaller banks with significant model risk. It "does not set forth enforceable standards", but supervisory action can still follow from unsafe or unsound model risk practices.

Can an AI system change a customer's due diligence level on its own?

Not under the EU AMLR from July 10, 2027: decisions to increase or decrease due diligence need meaningful human intervention. In the US, the FFIEC manual expects CDD procedures to set out "authority, and responsibility for reviewing and approving changes to a customer's risk profile".
